name: Hungry judge effect
statement: Israeli parole judges ruled for the prisoner in about 65% of cases at the start of a session and in almost none by its end.
meaning: The finding has a mechanism attached, and the mechanism is the contested part. Danziger, Levav and Avnaim-Pesso proposed that making one ruling after another depletes a judge's mental resources, and that a depleted judge falls back on the easier option. In a parole hearing the easier option is to deny, because denial preserves the status quo and takes less writing. A food break restores the resource and the grant rate jumps back. The popular version drops the mechanism and keeps the meal, which is how a paper about position in a queue became a paper about breakfast. What the authors measured was the ordinal position of a case within a session.

origin.who: Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav and Liora Avnaim-Pesso
origin.where: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Extraneous factors in judicial decisions" and opens by naming the caricature it sets out to test, that justice is what the judge ate for breakfast. It records the timing and length of two daily breaks, calls the morning one a snack of a sandwich and fruit served to the judge at the bench, and states that the data cannot test the breakfast claim directly.

evidence: 1,112 rulings by eight Jewish-Israeli judges sitting on two parole boards, collected over 50 days in a 10-month period. The boards handle about 40% of parole requests in the country. A judge heard 14 to 35 cases a day, an average of 22.58, each taking about six minutes. A morning snack and a lunch break split the day into three sessions, the first break falling after 7.8 cases on average and the second after 11.4. Overall 64.2% of requests were rejected, a figure that pools outright refusals with deferrals to a later hearing; deferrals are 48.4% of the reject category. The 65% and the near-zero endpoint appear in the abstract and in the sentence describing Figure 1, and both are given as approximations rather than as measured quantities. That graph plots the proportion of favourable rulings against ordinal position, and is drawn from the first 95% of each session because the later positions hold few cases. A fixed-effects logistic regression controlling for offence severity, months served, previous imprisonments, rehabilitation programme, sex and ethnicity put the coefficient on the first decision of the third session at 2.873 (SE 0.425) and the coefficient on overall decision count at -0.078 (SE 0.020). Favourable rulings took longer than unfavourable ones, 7.37 minutes against 5.21, and their written verdicts ran 89.61 words against 47.36.

replication.headline: A large American arraignment court shows a decline of about 6 percentage points across the hours before a meal and no rise after it, and an Arkansas traffic court shows a decline in arraignments but not in trials.
replication.detail: The dispute runs in three separate arguments. Weinshall-Margel and Shapard interviewed three attorneys, a parole panel judge and five prison service and court staff, and reported that case order is not random: a board tries to finish one prison before breaking and to start another after, and unrepresented prisoners usually go last. In their own 227 decisions from 12 hearing days, unrepresented prisoners were about a third of cases and prevailed 15% of the time against 35% for those with counsel; excluding deferrals those rates become 39% and 67%. Dropping deferrals from the original data, they put the within-session slide at about 75% falling to 42% rather than 65% falling to zero. They add that the ruling is made by a three-member panel of judge, criminologist and social worker rather than by a judge alone. Danziger and colleagues replied that they recoded the data with legal representation as a predictor and reran every model. Case order and the meal break stayed robust, the significant parameters were unchanged apart from months served, and representation itself was positively correlated with release without reaching significance in every model. Dropping deferrals as well left case order and the meal break robust. They counted 39 instances of an attorney holding two cases in a day and 4 of three, under one shared-counsel case a day against the 4.1 the letter reported, and on the five days where they know the prison of origin, prisoners from the same prison appear both before and after a break. They gave no revised effect size, which Chatziathanasiou treats as the weak point of the reply. Glöckner attacked the magnitude. A drop from 65% to 5% is an odds ratio of 35, or d = 1.96, which he sets against a publication-bias-corrected meta-analytic estimate for mental depletion of d = -0.10 to 0.25 and the 23-lab registered replication at d = 0.04, covered at entry no. 2 here. He then simulated a rational judge who declines to start a case she cannot finish before the break, using the ruling times the original paper reports, and produced a curve of similar shape from a 36% base rate. Censoring the last 5% of each session, as the original graph does, increased the simulated drop, and produced one of roughly 15% even when the simulated judge had no foresight. His simulated sessions opened at 45% rather than 65%, a shortfall he names, and he put the drop rational time management would generate at 15% to 45%. His claim is that the effect is overstated, not that it is absent. The field test is Shroff and Vamvourellis, who examined 96,318 pretrial arraignments heard by 41 judges, each of whom sat on at least 500, in a large urban American court system between 2010 and 2015. Covariate-adjusted release rates fell about 6 percentage points across the hours before lunch and before dinner, stayed flat through the rest of each session, and did not rise once judges had eaten: the half hour after lunch ran 0.5 percentage points above the half hour before it, p = 0.74, 95% CI -2 to 3 points. On the 39,157 arraignments from 2013 to 2015 carrying a recorded prosecution bail request, the rate at which judges agreed with that request moved with neither the time nor the break. Hemrajani and Hobert found charges less likely to be dismissed late in a session in Pulaski County traffic arraignments in 2019 and 2020, and no such pattern in trial hearings in the same court. Their full text sits behind the Cambridge paywall and was not open at Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, the authors' pages or the National Law School of India repository on 17 August 2026, so only the abstract was read. It gives no sample size and reports no test of a rebound after a break.

study.cite: Shroff, R., & Vamvourellis, K. (2022). Pretrial release judgments and decision fatigue. Judgment and Decision Making, 17(6), 1176-1207.

limits: A search of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar on 17 August 2026 found no repeat of the Israeli analysis on fresh Israeli parole data. Glöckner records that the data were not available to him, the authors being willing to share but blocked by those who first gave them access, so his critique simulates the process instead of reanalysing it. Daljord, Urminsky and Ureta thank Levav for the data, and the same search found no journal version of their reanalysis, which remains a preprint. It does not dispute the cyclical pattern and argues that the status quo account of depletion does not fit it. The nearest test of the food claim itself runs the other way. Mehmood, Seror and Chen used half a century of daily sentencing records from Pakistan and India, about half a million cases and 10,000 judges, and read the effect of fasting off the rotating Islamic calendar and the latitude of each district court. Fasting raised Muslim judges' acquittal rates and lowered their appeal and reversal rates. Their published text is paywalled, and only the abstract was read. The two field studies are not replications in the strict sense, because American pretrial arraignment and Arkansas traffic court differ from Israeli parole in stakes, in who controls the order and in what the default ruling is. Shroff and Vamvourellis do find a decline within a session, so their result is not a flat null. What they fail to find is the part that carries the depletion account, the rebound after eating.
misreadings: The paper does not record what any judge ate for breakfast, and it says its data cannot test the breakfast claim directly. What it records of the meals is the timing and length of the two breaks and a sandwich and fruit at the morning one. What it tested was position in a sequence. The near-zero endpoint is the tail of a plotted curve whose later positions hold few cases, not a finding that late applicants never win. Deferral to a later hearing is counted with rejection, which the authors defend as psychologically equivalent and Weinshall-Margel and Shapard reject as legally distinct. The critics also disagree with each other, and flattening them into one verdict misreports all three. Weinshall-Margel and Shapard call the post-break peak an artefact of case ordering. Glöckner argues the effect is overstated rather than absent, and says his account leaves parts of the pattern unexplained. Chatziathanasiou reports indications that the correlation was spurious and strong doubts about the study's validity, and his conclusion is narrower than either: that the study should not be used to argue for automated decision aids or other interventions in law. He adds that a flawed piece of evidence does not show judges cannot be biased.
